title: The site has its own name, mottos and icon
description:

title: Sketch annotations can spill out of the drawing
description:
Observed 2026-09-11 on the homepage feature: the bottom note of a project sketch
("ассистент действует прямо в прокрутке", 38 characters, well inside the
schema's 50) wrapped to a second line on a desktop and ran out of the drawing,
over the "Рассмотреть набросок" link. At 390 px the same text fit.

Three causes in `ExperimentSketch.astro`:

- the note's font size follows the viewport (`vw`), while the drawing's width
  follows its column — on a desktop the compact drawing is ~400 px wide and the
  font is sized for a wide window, so text that fits on a phone wraps;
- the bottom note is positioned from the top (`top: 91%`), so a second line
  grows downward out of the drawing;
- nothing limits the number of lines, so a note can also grow into the drawing.

Shortening the content hid it once. The layout itself must hold for any text
the schema accepts.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] With the longest annotation the schema allows, every note stays inside the drawing at 1440, 390 and 320 px, on the homepage and /projects/ (check-ui)
- [x] Top notes stay in the top band and the bottom note in the bottom band of the drawing (check-ui)
- [x] No note is clipped (check-ui)
- [x] A picture of any proportions keeps the drawing a square sheet, so the bands hold (check-ui, 3:1 picture)
- [x] `npm run verify` and check-ui green; the built-in plate still shows its arrows
close_reason: Notes sized in cqi on a square container sheet, anchored to their edges, clamped to 3/2 lines; check-ui with 50-char notes on a 3:1 picture green at 1440/390/320, verify 191 green, deployed and live-checked

title: Crawler surface: sitemap, robots.txt, favicon, SITE_URL gate
description:
The build emits `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, markdown twins, `/index.json` and
five RSS feeds. It does not emit the one file every ordinary crawler asks for.

- **No `sitemap.xml`.** `@astrojs/sitemap` is not installed.
- **No `robots.txt`.** There is no `public/` directory in the repository at all.
  It should point at the sitemap and at `/llms.txt`.
- **No favicon**, so every page load takes a 404 on `/favicon.ico`.
- **`SITE_URL` fails open.** `astro.config.mjs:9` is
  `process.env.SITE_URL ?? 'https://example.com'`. A build without the variable
  does not fail — it ships a site whose every `<link rel="canonical">`, every
  `hreflang`, and every absolute URL in `llms.txt`, `/index.json` and the feeds
  names `example.com`. A page declaring a foreign domain canonical is worse than
  a page declaring none, and it is precisely the silent per-address failure
  `scripts/check-outputs.ts` was written to refuse.

The gate belongs with R10's other checks: the placeholder is legitimate for
`astro build` in this repository, so `check-outputs.ts` — which runs on the
built artifact — is where it must be caught, not in the config.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] `dist/sitemap-index.xml` (or `sitemap.xml`) exists after a build and lists every indexable address
- [x] Draft, `/search/` and 404 addresses are absent from the sitemap, matching their `noindex`
- [x] `robots.txt` is served, references the sitemap absolutely, and points at `/llms.txt`
- [x] A favicon is served and referenced from `<head>`
- [x] `check-outputs.ts` fails a build whose canonical host is the `example.com` placeholder
- [x] That gate is proved by a test, not by reading the code
close_reason: Hand-rolled /sitemap.xml and /robots.txt endpoints rather than @astrojs/sitemap, because the plugin cannot know about noindex; a light/dark favicon.svg; and check-outputs.ts now fails a build whose canonical is the example.com placeholder, with CHECK_PLACEHOLDER_HOST=allow as the documented escape hatch for a local build. test/head.test.ts asserts set equality between the sitemap and the indexable addresses of a real build, and proves the gate by running it against a build made without SITE_URL.

title: Design system: the mark, the tag palette, the one real number
description:
The maintainer named a reference they call beautiful — maxtokens.ai — after
rejecting the terminal frame and the stripped-back version. Read what actually
makes it work rather than copying it: a wordmark that is a visual pun on the
subject, pastel tag chips, a sans UI, one computed number per row, a filter row
with counts, and a lot of air.

The mistake it exposed: three iterations optimised for honest and minimal, and
the ask was **beautiful**. danluu.com is respected for its writing, not admired
for its design; asking for one and building the other was the error.

What landed, and why each is specific to this site rather than borrowed:

- **The mark is the name over the corpus split into coloured counts.** Identity
  and filter in one object. The numbers are article counts, so the row's shape is
  the shape of what the author writes about, and it changes on its own as the
  archive grows. maxtokens' chips carry token ids because that site is about
  tokens; ours carry a taxonomy because this one is about a body of work.
- **Colour means exactly one thing: a tag.** Six pastels, stable per tag across
  every page, so the colour becomes a second name. This restores what the very
  first §12 asked for — pastel labels — which an earlier pass deleted wholesale.
- **One sans, monospace only for machine-produced values.** The serif read as
  "old blog", which is the opposite of the brief.
- **One number per row: the exact byte length of the markdown twin**, from
  `articleMarkdown()` — the same string the build emits at `/posts/<slug>.md`,
  not an estimate. This is the honest version of the fabricated telemetry that
  every rejected mockup leaned on: the form of instrumentation, with a figure
  that is completely true. Kilobytes rather than tokens because a token count
  needs a tokenizer and remains a guess about whose.
- **Three zones per row** — when, what, how much — metadata gathered at the right
  edge, the writing alone in the middle.

The mark is a component taking the name from `data/author.yaml`, because §2 says
this repository is an engine and carries no site of its own. It renders the
synthetic name until a content repository supplies a real one.

Trap worth recording: a prop named `as` makes astro check stop seeing the
component's `Props` interface entirely — callers then fail with "Property does
not exist on type 'IntrinsicAttributes'" and the component's own destructuring
reports implicit `any`. Renaming the prop fixed it; no cast or annotation did.

- [x] A tag renders the same colour on the front page, in a listing row and on an article
- [x] Every row shows the exact byte length of its markdown twin, computed from the same function the twin route uses

title: Phase 2: agent publishing pipeline
description:

title: Head: titles, Open Graph, Twitter cards
description:
`src/layouts/Base.astro` renders twelve lines of `<head>` and none of them tell a
social client, or a human reading a tab strip, whose site this is.

`<title>` is the bare page title (`Base.astro:48`), so the homepage is `Записи`
while its own `<h1>` says «Собираю свою цифровую жизнь», and `/search/`,
`/projects/`, `/about/` are indistinguishable from any site in existence. The
author's name is already in scope — `getAuthor()` at `Base.astro:33` feeds the
wordmark.

There is no `og:*` or `twitter:*` tag anywhere, so a link pasted into Telegram,
Slack or X unfurls as a bare URL. For a site that ships `Link: </llms.txt>` on
every response, having explained everything to agents and nothing to a person in
a chat window is a strange place to have landed.

Articles additionally have `date`, `updated`, `tags` and `author` on hand in
`Post.astro`, which is exactly what `article:published_time`,
`article:modified_time`, `article:tag` and `article:author` want.

Scope: `Base.astro` and the props `Post.astro` passes it. The image itself is
oh-my-portal-og-image.

- [x] The homepage title agrees with its own `<h1>` rather than contradicting it

- [x] `og:type`, `og:title`, `og:description`, `og:url`, `og:site_name`, `og:locale` and `og:image` render on every page
- [x] `twitter:card`, `twitter:title`, `twitter:description`, `twitter:image` render on every page

title: npm run dev does not show drafts
description:
`PREVIEW=1` is the flag that makes drafts visible (src/posts.ts), and no script
sets it. So the local dev server hides exactly the post being written, and the
only way to see a draft is the CI preview flow in §7 — a push, a build and a
deploy to look at a paragraph.

This is the piece the maintainer asked about when pointing at Astro's Jekyll
migration guide: Jekyll's `_drafts` are visible with `jekyll serve --drafts`, and
the local equivalent here is one word in package.json.

Two ways: `PREVIEW=1` in the `dev` script, so writing always shows drafts and
production never does; or a separate `dev:drafts`. The first is almost certainly
right — the dev server is where drafts are written, and the flag already cannot
leak into a production build because that runs a different script.

title: kind: note is declared and used nowhere
description:
`kind: article | note | page` is in the schema (§4), and `note` is inert: nothing
branches on it. `listPosts` excludes only `page`, so a note renders exactly like
an article — same listing row, same article layout.

Worse, the schema makes a short post expensive: `title` and `summary` are both
required, and `summary` is capped at 200 characters. Writing a three-sentence
note therefore costs a title, a one-sentence abstract of three sentences, and a
tag decision. That friction is aimed at exactly the posts meant to be cheap.

The maintainer wants both long articles and short notes. Decide:

- Does a note need a title? A dated note with no title is the usual shape, but
  the title feeds the listing, the feeds, /index.json and llms.txt — so removing
  it means those projections need a fallback, probably the first line.
- Does a note need a summary? It is one sentence and the note may be three.
- Does a note appear in the same listing as articles, in a separate stream, or
  interleaved with a different row treatment?
- Does a note get its own feed, so subscribers can take articles only?

Whatever is decided, it lands in §4 and in the schema together — a `kind` that
changes nothing is worse than no `kind`, because it looks like it does.

- [ ] §4 says what a note is, what it requires, and where it appears
- [ ] The schema makes required fields conditional on kind, or the decision to keep them is recorded with its reason
- [ ] The archive renders a note differently from an article, or the decision not to is recorded

title: nginx example served the whole site as octet-stream, and markdown without a charset
description:
Two faults in `nginx/site.conf.example`, found because the maintainer opened a
`.md` twin in a browser and got mojibake. Both were verified against a real
nginx 1.30.4 rather than reasoned about, and both are fixed.

**1. `types` inside `server` replaced the MIME map instead of extending it.**

    types { text/markdown md; }

A `types` block in a nested context does not add to the map inherited from
`include mime.types` — it replaces it. Measured: with that block inside the
server, `a.css` came back as `application/octet-stream`. In production every
stylesheet, script, font and image would have gone out with the wrong type, and
a browser refuses CSS served that way. The site would have rendered unstyled on
its first deploy, and nothing in the repository would have said why.

Moved to the top level of the file, beside the `map`. A conf.d file is included
inside `http`, so there the block extends the map: `a.css` → `text/css`,
`b.md` → `text/markdown`.

**2. No charset on markdown.**

The files on disk are UTF-8; the header said only `text/markdown`, so a browser
fell back to its own default and Cyrillic arrived as `Ð‘Ñ�ÐºÐ°Ð¿`. Fixed with
`charset utf-8` plus a `charset_types` list that names `text/markdown` — nginx
charsets `text/html` unconditionally and nothing else unless it is listed.
`text/html` is deliberately absent from that list because including it only
produces a duplicate-type warning.

Verified end to end on a running nginx: css `text/css; charset=utf-8`, twin
`text/markdown; charset=utf-8`, `/about/` under `Accept: text/markdown`
`text/markdown; charset=utf-8`, under `Accept: text/html` `text/html;
charset=utf-8`, and Cyrillic round-tripping intact.

**Why nothing caught it.** `test/helpers.ts` serves the built site for the tests
and its own type map omitted the charset in exactly the same way, so a test
server more forgiving than production hid the bug it was meant to expose. It now
sends charsets too.

`test/nginx.test.ts` gates the config: the mapping exists, it is declared before
the server block, a charset is set, `charset_types` names markdown, and `Vary:
Accept` survives. Mutation-checked — reintroducing both faults fails exactly the
two relevant assertions.

Known and not fixable here: `astro preview` drops a prerendered endpoint's
headers, so a `.md` twin still looks like mojibake locally. Recorded in
CLAUDE.md, with the note that nginx over `dist` is what to check instead.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] A stylesheet is served as text/css by the shipped config, verified against a running nginx
- [x] A markdown twin is served as text/markdown with charset=utf-8
- [x] A negotiated directory address returns markdown with a charset under Accept: text/markdown
- [x] Cyrillic content round-trips through the server unchanged
- [x] The test server sends the same charsets production does
- [x] A test fails if the types block moves into the server block or the charset is dropped
- [x] The preview-server limitation is written down where someone will hit it

description:

The code was written so that either answer works: src/redirects.ts is a generic library (expand/validate/render), scripts/gen-redirects.ts takes the map path and the output path as arguments, and the map only has to move. If it moves, test/redirects.test.ts splits too: the engine tests the library against fixtures, the content repository tests its own map for exhaustiveness.

Second, separate question: the file is already in git history across three commits of a public repository. Moving it forward does not remove it from the past. Rewriting history is the maintainer's call.

title: The deployed site is served uncompressed: gzip is off in the CDN
description:
Every object in the bucket is served with `Content-Encoding: aws-chunked`, and
as a result **nothing on the site is compressed** — not the HTML, not the CSS.

Measured against the live deploy, asking for it explicitly:

```
curl -I -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip, br' <site>/
  content-length: 27938
  content-encoding: aws-chunked      # no gzip, no br

curl -I -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip, br' <site>/_astro/<hash>.css
  content-length: 6085
  content-encoding: aws-chunked
```

A 28 KB HTML document that should leave the edge at roughly a quarter of that,
on every page view. The `immutable` month-long cache on the assets does not help
the first visit, which is the one that decides whether a reader stays.

## Cause

`aws-chunked` is not a content encoding a client can decode — it is the AWS
CLI's *upload* transfer framing for streaming checksums. Recent AWS CLI v2
calculates a checksum on every upload by default and sends
`Content-Encoding: aws-chunked` with it. Our storage stores that header as
object metadata instead of consuming it, so it is echoed back on every GET, and
the CDN will not compress a response that already declares an encoding.

Prime suspect, not yet verified: `AWS_REQUEST_CHECKSUM_CALCULATION=when_required`
in the environment `scripts/deploy-s3.ts` builds for the CLI, which keeps the
CLI off the chunked-checksum upload path. The alternative — a metadata-rewriting
pass that clears `Content-Encoding` after upload — treats the symptom and has to
run forever.

## Notes

- Fixing the script does not fix the objects already in the bucket. The first
  pass of `deploy-s3.ts` re-copies the whole tree, so one deploy after the fix
  repairs it — but only if the CLI genuinely stops sending the header. Verify on
  a single object before re-deploying everything.
- Purge the CDN afterwards, as the script's closing note says.
- This is invisible in a browser: the page renders correctly and only weighs
  four times what it should. It was found by asking for gzip with curl, which is
  the only way to see it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ask the deployed site for a compressed response and look at what comes back:

   ```
   curl -sI -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip, br' <site>/ | grep -i 'content-encoding\|content-length'
   ```

2. Observed: `content-encoding: aws-chunked` and the full uncompressed length.
   Expected: `content-encoding: gzip` and roughly a quarter of it.
3. Repeat against any `/_astro/*.css` asset — the same result, so it is not
   specific to HTML.

Nothing is needed but curl. A browser shows the page rendering correctly and
gives no sign of it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] GZip is enabled on the CDN resource and the cache purged in full
- [x] `curl -I -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip'` against the deployed HTML returns `content-encoding: gzip`
- [x] The CSS and JS assets are compressed too, not only the HTML
- [x] It is established whether aws-chunked also blocks compression, and if it does, a freshly uploaded object carries no such header
- [x] Whatever was learned is recorded in the header comment of `scripts/deploy-s3.ts`, beside the three failures already documented there
- [x] `/rss/index.html`, written by its own pass after the delete, is covered as well
acceptance_criteria:
- [x] GZip is enabled on the CDN resource and the cache purged in full
- [x] `curl -I -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip'` against the deployed HTML returns `content-encoding: gzip`
- [x] The CSS and JS assets are compressed too, not only the HTML
- [x] It is established whether aws-chunked also blocks compression, and if it does, a freshly uploaded object carries no such header
- [x] Whatever was learned is recorded in the header comment of `scripts/deploy-s3.ts`, beside the three failures already documented there
- [x] `/rss/index.html`, written by its own pass after the delete, is covered as well
notes:
Diagnosis corrected before any work started: gzip compression is simply OFF in
the CDN resource settings. The panel has three switches on its content tab —
"Сжатие GZip" (off), "Запрашивать сжатие на источнике" (off, and correctly so:
the origin is object storage and cannot compress on the fly) and Brotli (off,
and gated behind origin shielding plus a support request).

So the cheap cause was found before the expensive one. Order of work:

1. Enable GZip in the CDN resource, save, purge the cache in full. Without the
   purge the edge keeps serving the objects it already cached uncompressed, and
   it looks like the switch did nothing.
2. Re-measure. `content-encoding: gzip` and roughly 7-8 KB on the front page
   instead of 27938 bytes.
3. Only then is it known whether aws-chunked was a second layer. If the response
   is still uncompressed and still declares aws-chunked, the edge is refusing to
   compress a response that already claims an encoding, and deploy-s3.ts has to
   stop sending it. If gzip arrives, the header was cosmetic and this issue
   drops to P2 — worth cleaning, not worth blocking on.

Brotli is a later refinement: 15-20% over gzip on text, but it needs shielding
and a support ticket, so it is not part of the fix.
Measured, not reasoned about. A controlled probe: the same 7129-byte text object
uploaded twice, once with the CLI default and once with
`AWS_REQUEST_CHECKSUM_CALCULATION=when_required`.

  stored metadata   default -> ContentEncoding: 'aws-chunked'
                    fixed   -> ContentEncoding: None
  over the wire     default -> 7129 bytes, content-encoding: aws-chunked
                    fixed   -> 2346 bytes, content-encoding: gzip

So both halves were real and neither works alone: gzip was off on the CDN *and*
the header blocked compression once it was on. Enabling gzip alone changed
nothing, which is what made the first diagnosis look wrong.

Done: the fix is in `scripts/deploy-s3.ts` as `CHECKSUM_ENV`, with the reasoning
in the header comment beside the other three failures. The site has been
re-deployed from a build byte-identical to the one already live (verified by
ETag before uploading, so this was a metadata repair and not a content change).
Origin metadata now reads `ContentEncoding: None` on HTML, CSS, the twins, both
copies of the feed and the article pages.

Remaining: a **full CDN cache purge**. Fresh paths through the edge already come
back gzipped; entries already cached still serve the old uncompressed objects,
and the hashed assets carry a month-long `immutable`, so they will not expire on
their own. After the purge, re-measure the front page and one `_astro/*.css`.
close_reason: Two independent causes, both fixed and both measured: gzip was off on the CDN resource (enabled by the maintainer), and the CLI's default streaming checksum left Content-Encoding: aws-chunked on every object, which stopped the edge compressing even once gzip was on. Fix is CHECKSUM_ENV in scripts/deploy-s3.ts; the site was re-deployed from a build verified byte-identical to the live one, then the cache purged. Front page 27938 -> 8178, stylesheet 6085 -> 1586. The build ships no JS at all, so that half of the criterion is vacuous. Feeds remain uncompressed because application/rss+xml is not on the CDN's MIME list — split out as oh-my-portal-k2v.

title: Phase 1d: ai-first tooling
description:
A typical agent arrives via one link, makes one request and leaves. It does not browse, does not see buttons, does not guess addresses. Priority follows from that.

1. Content negotiation on the same URL: Accept: text/markdown returns the agent version. Coding assistants already send that header, so it needs no cooperation. nginx map over two build trees; Vary: Accept is mandatory or caches will hand markdown to browsers.
2. Structured core (recipe) as the first block of an article, in both versions.
3. Twins at direct addresses: /<slug>.md, /<slug>.json, /index.json, /llms.txt, plus <link rel=alternate>.
4. Link header advertising llms.txt on every response.

R10: a build that does not emit all three outputs has failed.

Not doing: MCP or OpenAPI for readers — both require someone to wire up a client first.

title: Design the URL scheme, redirect map and frontmatter schema
description:
Precondition for all of phase 1.

1. URL scheme. Do not inherit Ghost's shape: articles sit at bare root there, so sections compete with slugs, and its slugs are transliterated Russian. New scheme: articles under /posts/<slug>/, plus /tag/, /about/, /projects/, /search/. Endpoints (/rss/, /llms.txt, /index.json, /webmentions/) are not content and take no language prefix.

/aboutme/ gets no special treatment: it is content, so it moves to /about/ and redirects like everything else. 'Already indexed' is true of every address here, and every address is being redirected anyway.

2. Language: prefixDefaultLocale false, per Astro's own recommendation. The default language has no prefix (/about/), additional ones do (/en/about/). An earlier draft argued for /ru/ from day one on the grounds that adding a segment later forces a second migration — that was wrong. With the default locale unprefixed there is no second migration either: Russian keeps its addresses and English, if it ever appears, arrives at /en/ without touching a single existing URL. Upside is real: shorter addresses for the language carrying all the traffic, and the framework's happy path instead of custom routing. lang stays authoritative in frontmatter, hreflang per page with x-default on the unprefixed tree.

3. Redirect mechanism. Astro's redirects config is NOT used. Its docs: astro build 'will output HTML files with the meta refresh tag by default' and 'if building to HTML files the status code is not used by the server'. Only supported adapters write real host config, and those exist for platforms ruled out on regional reachability. So the redirect map is a data file and a build step emits nginx configuration from it: one source of truth, real status codes, no dead meta-refresh pages.

4. Redirect map. Export every existing article URL and map it to its new address. 301 not 302, one hop only, never through an intermediate. Exhaustive — organic search is the only working distribution channel. /rss/ is the single exemption, for a mechanical reason: feed readers handle moved feeds unreliably and some drop the subscription silently.

5. Slug rewrite. Every address is being redirected anyway, so slugs are rewritten now: short, lowercase, readable, naming the subject rather than transliterating a headline. Free at migration time, expensive at any other.

6. CI test, two assertions per old address: the old one returns 301 with Location pointing at the new one, and the new one returns 200. Plus: no redirect target is itself a redirect.

7. Zod schema for Astro Content Collections: required (title, slug, date, kind, status, author, summary, tags, lang) and optional (aliases, updated, tools, sources, related, recipe).

Spec: docs/design/portal.md sections 3-5.

title: Ghost importer: 21 articles into the content repository
description: The larger half of 8y2: the articles themselves. A one-time operation, run locally against the Ghost Admin API, NOT part of any deploy pipeline. The tool lives in the engine (importing from Ghost is a capability of an engine that replaces Ghost); its output lives in the private content repository. Measured shape of the source, 2026-09-10: - 21 posts, **no drafts** - 90 `` in bodies: 41 on the author's own host, 49 hotlinked elsewhere - 27 of those are `kg-bookmark-icon` — favicons inside Ghost bookmark cards, not illustrations at all - alt text on **3 images out of 90** - `custom_excerpt` on 7 posts out of 21 - bodies from 288 to 54571 characters Decisions taken (maintainer, 2026-09-10): 1. Images live at `images//` and are referenced by **absolute** path `/images//file.png`. The `.md` twin is the source body verbatim (§6), so nothing rewrites paths and nothing can drift. 2. The 41 own images are downloaded and compressed at import time. 3. The 49 hotlinks become **text links**. Nothing third-party is rehosted, and no reader is tracked by a foreign server on page view. 4. `feature_image` is **not** migrated. §12 forbids decorative illustration and the og card is one drawn card for the whole site. Consequences that need human work, not code: - 14 posts need a `summary` written by hand: the schema requires it, caps it at 200 characters, and Ghost's auto-excerpt is the first paragraph truncated. - alt text is missing almost everywhere. Whatever `xts` settles as the alt rule, roughly 40 captions have to be written by a person. - Ghost bodies are Lexical rendered to HTML; header cards, image cards, bookmark cards and callouts have no markdown equivalent and each needs a decision. Slugs and tags are not invented here: `migration/redirects.yaml` already maps all 21 old slugs to new ones and collapses 20 tags into 6. The importer reads that file rather than duplicating the decision. ## Acceptance Criteria - [ ] The raw Ghost export is preserved in the content repository, so the import can be re-run without the live blog - [ ] All 21 posts land as markdown whose frontmatter validates against the schema - [ ] Slugs and tags come from migration/redirects.yaml, and a post whose slug is missing from it fails loudly - [ ] The 41 own images are downloaded to images// and referenced by absolute path - [ ] No hotlink to a third-party image survives in any body - [ ] No feature_image reaches the frontmatter - [ ] Posts still needing a hand-written summary are listed by the tool rather than filled with a placeholder that ships
notes:
2026-09-10: scope corrected twice in one session, both by measurement rather than by reading.

First: the count is not 21. `3d-modieli-dlia-piechati` is a *page* in Ghost, not a post, so anything iterating `posts` would have silently dropped it while the redirect map still pointed at it.

Then the maintainer settled it the other way: **that article is not migrated at all.** So the import IS 21 articles, and the tool must read `posts` only — but the old address still has to resolve, because the sitemap knows it. It now redirects to /archive/ from the `pages` section. 410 would be the honest answer and is unavailable: every section of the map renders a 301, and object storage routing rules cannot return anything but a redirect.

Also measured, and it changes what the importer can promise about tags:

- Only 5 of the 6 declared tags survive the mechanical mapping, and their counts are half what migration/redirects.yaml claims in its comment: pkms 5, homelab 3, kubernetes 3, ai-agents 2, security 2 — against the stated 7/6/4/3/3/2.
- **12 of the 22 entries get no tag at all.** `kubernetes-pod-logs` and `kubernetes-descheduler` carry no Ghost tag whatsoever despite being plainly Kubernetes articles.
- `blogging` is the target of no mapping. It is a hand assignment to two posts and cannot be derived.
- Three `hash-import-*` tags are Ghost internals, never addresses, correctly excluded.

So tagging cannot be fully mechanical. Either the thin result is accepted, or a human passes over 21 articles — the importer should not invent tags either way, and this is the maintainer's open decision.
2026-09-10: importer built and run end to end. scripts/import-ghost.ts, three stages: fetch, images, convert.

Landed in the content repository: migration/ghost-export.json (1.5 MB, html AND lexical, the only copy once Ghost is off), the four old sitemaps, 36 images at images/<slug>/NN.webp with a manifest, 21 articles at posts/<slug>.md, and data/{author,projects}.yaml.

Verified by building, not by reading: 25 pages in production (7 published), 54 with PREVIEW=1 (all 21), R10 output gate clean, npm run verify 0 errors over 84 files and 149 tests, and the front page plus an article looked at in a browser at desktop and phone width.

Two defects the work exposed, both fixed:
1. The image stage rewrote its manifest from scratch each run. These hosts time out at random, so a rerun was never a superset of the previous one and the manifest SHRANK — 35 files on disk, 33 in the manifest, and the convert stage would have turned the difference into broken links. Now it resumes and retries three times.
2. Content images were referenced but never copied into the build: 36 broken pictures and nothing failed. An astro:build:done integration copies IMAGES_DIR, and check-outputs.ts now fails the build on any /images/ reference with no file behind it.

Decisions made while converting, each recorded next to its code: bookmark cards become plain links (they carried 54 of the 90 images as decoration); header cards become h2; callouts become blockquotes; Telegram comment widgets are dropped and reported; internal links on the old domain are rewritten through the redirect map, including one surviving /blog/<slug> form.

Excerpt handling: 7 articles had a hand-written excerpt, 3 of those over the schema's 200 characters. Those are cut at a sentence boundary — the author's own words, never rewritten — and every cut is printed for review. The other 14 have NO usable summary and are imported as status: draft, so they cannot reach production until a human writes one. That is the schema and §4 doing the gating rather than a TODO nobody greps for.

title: The one directory an agent may not change, kept where the agent cannot reach it
description:
`scripts/check-agent-paths.ts`: given the files a branch changed, refuse any change to the content repository's pipeline, `.github/**`.

It lives **here**, in the public engine repository, on purpose. The agent's token reaches the content repository only, so a rule kept here is one it cannot edit. A rule kept beside the articles could be rewritten by the same token that writes them, and the boundary would exist only in the paperwork (design §9).

One refusal rather than an allowlist, by the maintainer's decision of 2026-09-11. Every other change reaches production only through the maintainer's merge. The pipeline is the one place where a branch's change takes effect before anyone merges it: a pull request from a branch runs that branch's workflows with the repository's secrets, so an agent that can edit them can grant itself the storage keys in one commit. The earlier allowlist protected nothing the merge does not already protect, and it kept the agent from maintaining project pages.

The refusal carries its reason in the code, because a rule whose reason is not written down is a rule someone deletes in a year.

The workflow that calls it belongs to the content repository and is tracked there.

title: Screenshot script, and the three things it caught
description:
The terminal redesign shipped twice without anyone looking at it, and both times
it was wrong in ways that a single screenshot would have shown in a second. Fixed
the cause first: `scripts/screenshot.ts` plus `npm run screenshot`.

On NixOS the browsers come from the nix store and its chromium build does not
match the revision the npm package expects, so `npx playwright install` is a trap
— it downloads a browser that will not start. The script resolves the binary out
of `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` and hands it to playwright directly, which skips
the revision check. CLAUDE.md carries that, along with two other things that cost
time this session: `preview` serves `dist` and shows nothing new until a rebuild,
and `verify` racing a running `dev` server dies on an unrelated filesystem error.

What the screenshots then showed, all three of them regressions from the identity
change (oh-my-portal-0zb):

1. `--frame: 62rem` put a path on the left and its date on the right with half a
   screen of nothing between them. They stopped reading as one row. Now 48rem —
   still wider than the reading column, so a status line still crosses the page.
2. The front page had no entry point: it opened on a line of small grey
   monospace. The heading was hidden behind `.sr-only` on the theory that the
   prompt line named the page. The highlight behind the heading was the thing
   worth removing; the heading was not. It is back, and `.sr-only` is gone.
3. The listing indented each summary by 2ch, the way `ls -R` indents. On screen
   that is a third left edge under a flush path and a flush title, and it reads
   as a mistake. Removed, and titles went from --step-1 to --step-2 so the page
   has something dark to land on.

Also: the `/` hint is hidden below 34rem, because a keyboard shortcut is worth
nothing to a thumb.

description:

deliberately ships without one: the being's state file does not exist yet, and a

every mockup in the design review was rejected for.

The shape agreed in that session:

- The being writes a small whitelisted JSON straight into the served directory —
  energy, count of live commitments, last activity. No commit, no rebuild, no
  deploy. §6a is untouched: nginx serving a file somebody else overwrites is not
  dynamic behaviour, so nothing moves into an application.
- The same file is the agent-facing artifact (§6), so one request serves both the
  human widget and somebody else's agent.
- The static HTML carries the last build's snapshot as the fallback, and the
  fetch replaces it. Without JS, and for an agent, a dated snapshot shows rather
  than an empty hole.

  state a month old is the lie this whole design is organised against.
- Whitelist, never blacklist: the being models its owner (user model, memories,
  message content). Only its reasoning *about itself* may be published. A
  blacklist eventually misses a field added six months later.

title: The redirect renderer emits nginx config, and the deploy is object storage
description:
`src/redirects.ts` has one renderer, `render()`, and it emits nginx `location`
blocks. That was correct while §7 deployed behind nginx. It no longer is: the
site is served from S3-compatible object storage behind a CDN
(ADR-0001), and that storage expresses redirects as `RoutingRules` in the
bucket's website configuration — a JSON document of `{Condition:
{KeyPrefixEquals}, Redirect: {ReplaceKeyWith | ReplaceKeyPrefixWith,
HttpRedirectCode}}`.

So today the map is validated, rendered, and rendered into a format nothing in
the deployment reads. **R1 is not actually deployed** — 45 redirects exist as
nginx configuration for a server that does not run. Nobody would notice from the
tests, which check that the nginx output is correct, and it is.

Both renderers are wanted, not one instead of the other: the nginx output stays
for whoever self-hosts the engine (§7 keeps that path deliberately), and the
routing-rules output is what our own deploy needs.

Things that will not map cleanly and need deciding rather than assuming:

- The nginx renderer emits **two** locations per address, slashed and unslashed.
  Object storage normalises the missing slash itself with a 302 — measured. So
  the unslashed half is unnecessary there, but the code it comes back as is 302,
  and §5 says 301 only. Whether that matters for an address nobody links to
  without a slash is a judgement call, not a fact.
- `KeyPrefixEquals` is a *prefix* match, not an exact one. Every rule in this map
  is exact, and a prefix rule matching more than intended is the kind of error
  that silently redirects a page that should have stayed. The renderer has to
  either prove exactness or refuse.
- Rule ordering is significant, and the documentation contradicts itself on
  whether the first or the last match wins. It has to be measured.
- The bucket already returns **403 rather than 404** for a missing key
  (`vk-hosting-findings-vn2`), and one routing-rule condition is
  `HttpErrorCodeReturnedEquals`. That may be the lever that fixes the status
  code, which would make this issue the place where that gets solved too.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] `renderS3()` emits two objects per live redirect, `<path>/index.html` and the bare key; the nginx `render()` still works and is still tested
- [x] A redirect whose source is a page in the build fails generation, naming the address
- [x] A redirect whose target is not in the build is held back, listed in the log and the job summary, and not emitted
- [x] `deploy-s3.ts --redirects` uploads the objects before the delete pass, and the delete pass excludes every manifest key and `rss/index.html`
- [x] `LONG` cache applies only to `_astro/`; content images, `og.png`, the favicon and Pagefind get `SHORT`
- [x] `scripts/check-live.ts` passes against a real deployment: every manifest object 301 to its target, every target 200, `/rss/` 200
- [x] `deploy-s3.ts` and `check-live.ts` import only `node:*`, enforced by a test
acceptance_criteria:
- [x] `renderS3()` emits two objects per live redirect, `<path>/index.html` and the bare key; the nginx `render()` still works and is still tested
- [x] A redirect whose source is a page in the build fails generation, naming the address
- [x] A redirect whose target is not in the build is held back, listed in the log and the job summary, and not emitted
- [x] `deploy-s3.ts --redirects` uploads the objects before the delete pass, and the delete pass excludes every manifest key and `rss/index.html`
- [x] `LONG` cache applies only to `_astro/`; content images, `og.png`, the favicon and Pagefind get `SHORT`
- [x] `scripts/check-live.ts` passes against a real deployment: every manifest object 301 to its target, every target 200, `/rss/` 200
- [x] `deploy-s3.ts` and `check-live.ts` import only `node:*`, enforced by a test
notes:
The shape is now decided and measured. The content repository carries the plan
(its `docs/plans/`, tracked in its own `br` as the epic "Publishing becomes git
push"); this issue is the engine half.

Measured against the real storage before planning, so none of this is assumed:
a zero-byte object with `--website-redirect-location` answers **301** and the CDN
expands it to an absolute URL preserving the Host; `curl -L` reports one hop and
a final 200; `put-object` needs no `--body`.

The one subtlety: **two keys per address.** The index resolver answers `/old/`
from `old/index.html`, but `/old` without the trailing slash gets a **302** to
`/old/` first — two hops and the first a 302, both of which R1 forbids. A bare
key alongside it answers that form directly with a 301. The nginx renderer
already emits both forms; the object emitter must match it.

And the ordering: redirect objects upload **after** the delete pass. They are
not in `dist`, so a `sync --delete` running afterwards removes every one of them
on every deploy — the same trap `/rss/index.html` already sits outside.
Stress-test site-03w (2026-09-11): the shape is per-object redirects, not RoutingRules — the analysis above of prefix matching and rule order no longer applies. The content repository's plan, Task 2, carries the code.

title: Copy button and a code block wide enough to read
description:
Two faults the maintainer found by looking at the code article shipped in
oh-my-portal-zdu: no way to copy a block, and code clipped at the reading
measure so the end of a command was not visible.

**Code breaks out of the reading column.** Prose wants 34rem and code does not —
a command is one line whether or not it fits, and clipping it at the measure
hides the end of the thing a reader came for. A block now widens to `--frame` and
no further; below that width the expression collapses back to the column so
nothing overflows the page. Long lines still scroll, which is right for shell.

**Each block gets a header: the language on the left, a copy button on the
right.** A header rather than a floating button, because a button over the block
covers its first line, which in a shell block is the command. The language comes
from `data-language`, which Shiki already emits and nothing was using.

Both are built by script, for the same reason the search box is: the clipboard
needs JavaScript, and a button that cannot do its job is worse than no button.
Without JavaScript a block is still a block — selectable, scrollable, and
promising nothing.

The trap, and it cost a round trip: **article HTML arrives through `<slot />` and
the wrapper is created at runtime, so neither carries the component's scope
attribute.** Every scoped selector aimed at them matched nothing and failed
silently — a header the width of its own text over a block that never widened.
They all need `:global`, like the heading markers already did.

Verified with playwright against the running build: three blocks wrapped,
languages read as bash/yaml/bash, the clipboard contents equal the block text
exactly, and the button shows `скопировано` after the click.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] A code block is wider than the prose column and never wider than the frame
- [x] On a narrow screen the block collapses to the column and the page does not scroll sideways
- [x] Each block shows its language and a copy button
- [x] Clicking copy puts the block's exact text on the clipboard, verified by a browser, not by inspection
- [x] The button reports success, and reports failure honestly when the clipboard is refused
- [x] The button's text is kept out of the search index
- [x] With JavaScript off there is no button and the block still works
- [x] npm run verify passes

- [x] On a narrow screen the block collapses to the column and the page does not scroll sideways
- [x] Each block shows its language and a copy button

notes: 2026-09-09: the breakout was wrong and the maintainer caught it. Widening a block to the frame bought a few characters and cost the page its left edge — prose starting in one place and every code block in another, on a site that is about reading. Reverted: blocks sit in the reading column like everything else, and long lines wrap with a hanging indent on Shiki's per-line spans, so a continuation reads as the same command rather than a second one. Two things had to be got right for that: pre { margin: 0 } inside the wrapper, or the browser default opened a white band between the header and the code; and white-space collapsing on the wrapper with pre-wrap on each line, because Shiki leaves a newline text node beside each line block and every block came out double-spaced. A transformer filtering those nodes had no effect — the CSS split is what works. Blank source lines keep their height through a zero-width character on :empty. Re-verified in a browser: no horizontal scroll, block height 242 to 202, clipboard still exact.

title: Split content into a private repository
description:
The engine stays public in oh-my-portal; articles move to a separate private repository.

Why: it turns the agent's permission boundary from a CI check we wrote into a credential the platform enforces — the agent's token reaches the content repository only and cannot touch templates, workflows, deploy settings or secrets. It also makes drafts private by construction rather than by discipline.

Work:
1. Create the private content repository with content/posts/, its own CI (build + deploy) and a deploy key.
2. Publish the engine as a git dependency: "oh-my-portal": "github:<owner>/oh-my-portal#<tag>". No npm publishing needed. Tag the engine; bumping the tag is the upgrade, and a broken engine commit cannot break publishing.
3. Issue the agent a token scoped to the content repository only.
4. Keep this repository free of real articles. Add a documented schema and two deliberately synthetic posts under examples/ so a visitor sees how content is shaped.
5. Keep engine issues in br here; content needs no tracker — a branch per article is the unit.

Cost to accept: the build needs two checkouts, and local engine work wants npm link.

Spec: docs/design/portal.md sections 2, 9.

title: Staging mode: a rehearsal copy must not be indexed
description:
The migration will be rehearsed on a subdomain before the apex is switched over,
and the engine has no way to say "this build is not the real site".

`src/pages/robots.txt.ts` emits `Allow: /` and an absolute `Sitemap:` line
unconditionally. A full copy of the articles on a staging host is therefore
indexable, and it would compete first with the live Ghost site at the old
address and then with the new one. The same articles on two hosts is precisely
the duplication the 49-entry redirect map exists to prevent — losing rankings to
the rehearsal rather than to the move would be an expensive irony.

§7 already assumes this mode for preview deploys ("wildcard vhost, basic-auth,
noindex"), but that was written for nginx. On a CDN in front of object storage
there is no basic-auth to lean on, so the `noindex` has to come out of the build
itself.

Shape, following the two switches this repository already has (`PREVIEW=1` for
drafts, the `SITE_URL` gate in `scripts/check-outputs.ts`):

- `STAGING=1` makes `/robots.txt` emit `Disallow: /` and drop the `Sitemap:` line
- every page carries `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` — `Base.astro`
  already takes a `noindex` prop, so this is one default rather than a new
  mechanism
- the state is visible on the page, not only in the markup: a rehearsal that
  looks identical to production is a rehearsal someone will mistake for it

Worth deciding while implementing: whether `check-outputs.ts` should refuse a
build that sets neither `STAGING=1` nor a real `SITE_URL`, the way it already
refuses the `example.com` placeholder in canonical. The failure mode it guards
against is the same one — a build that ships with the wrong identity.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `STAGING=1` yields `Disallow: /` in /robots.txt and no `Sitemap:` line
- [ ] Every page in a staging build carries a noindex robots meta tag
- [ ] A production build is unchanged: `Allow: /`, the sitemap advertised, no noindex
- [ ] A test asserts both halves against real builds, as `test/build.test.ts` does for drafts
- [ ] The staging state is visible to a human looking at the page

title: JSON-LD: BlogPosting, WebSite, Person, BreadcrumbList
description:
An article already carries `date`, `updated`, `author`, `tags`, `tools`,
`sources` and the sha256 of its markdown twin. All of it reaches `/posts/<slug>.md`
and `/index.json`, which no search engine reads, and none of it reaches the HTML
in a machine-readable form.

`schema.org` markup is the format those readers do parse, and every field it
wants is already computed in `Post.astro` — this is assembling data that exists,
not gathering new data.

- `BlogPosting` on an article: headline, description, datePublished,
  dateModified, author, keywords, inLanguage, mainEntityOfPage.
- `WebSite` + `Person` on the homepage, from the content repository's author.
- `BreadcrumbList` on `/posts/<slug>/` and `/tag/<tag>/`.

The author fields must degrade rather than invent: `getAuthor()` returns
`undefined` when no content repository is mounted (`src/site.ts:16`), and a
JSON-LD block naming nobody is better than one naming a placeholder.

Depends on oh-my-portal-5og only for not colliding in `Base.astro`.

- [x] An article page emits one `BlogPosting` block with headline, description, datePublished, inLanguage and keywords from its own frontmatter
- [x] `dateModified` appears only when the post has `updated`
- [x] The homepage emits `WebSite`, and `Person` only when an author is available
- [x] `/posts/<slug>/` and `/tag/<tag>/` emit a `BreadcrumbList`

title: Article page: top line, markdown markers, and a provenance page
description:
Applies the reference's article page. Three things landed, all of them facts the
build can compute rather than decoration.

**The top line, above the title.** Date, tag chips, and the twin's exact byte
length — the same three values the archive row carries, in the same order, so an
article and its line in the listing agree about what it is. `обновлено` and the
`author: being` byline moved below the title: neither is how a reader decides
whether to start.

**Headings carry their own markdown marker.** `##` before an h2, `###` before an
h3, generated by CSS so the marker can never disagree with the level. It is not
an ornament borrowed from the reference: §1 makes a markdown file the source of
truth and §6 serves that file at an address one click away, so showing the `##`
says what the page actually is.

**`/posts/<slug>/integrity/` — provenance for one article.** The sha256 of
exactly what `/posts/<slug>.md` serves, plus the commits that touched the file.
Both are checkable from outside the site, which is the only kind of claim worth
publishing about oneself:

    curl -s https://<site>/posts/<slug>.md | sha256sum

Verified against a running build: the page's hash and the served twin's hash
match, and the revision list renders from real `git log` output.

The hash is taken over `articleMarkdown()` rather than over the source file,
because the twin is what is published. History comes from git run in the file's
own directory — the engine builds against a content checkout it does not own
(§2). An empty history is a normal answer (shallow clone, tarball, uncommitted
file) and the page says so rather than inventing a row.

Also: prev/next at the end of an article, and the R10 twin for the new address,
without which check-outputs.ts would have failed the build.

Supersedes oh-my-portal-q6y, which asked for a commit hash in the provenance
line. A page is the better shape: the line stays short, and the full hash and the
whole history have somewhere to live.

description:
Applies the design agreed in the session that reviewed five mockups. The
synthesis: the terminal idiom supplies the **frame**, the existing §12 tokens
supply the palette, and prose keeps the text face.

What is taken from where:

- The tmux identity lives entirely in a **status line**, not in panes. Panes
  break R1 (every article is an address), the back button, and mobile, and a
  hand-written pane manager is exactly the code §12 says will rot.
- The archive becomes a **directory listing** — path, date, title, summary,
  state — instead of cards. No border, no radius, no shadow anywhere.
- A **provenance line** under the article title, built only from fields the

- Reading time computed from the body word count. Real, not decorative.
- `/` focuses search, or goes to /search/ when the box is elsewhere. What makes

- No right rail for the being's state. `/being.json` does not exist yet

title: A deploy deletes the stylesheet that cached pages still link to
description:
Observed 2026-09-11 on the rehearsal domain: `/archive/` rendered without styles.
The CDN served its HTML from a cache filled at 08:11, which links
`/_astro/Base.DQLVMF7A.css`; the 08:56 deploy had built `Base.BGJGKpqM.css` and
its delete pass removed the old file, so the link answered 403.

Two things combine:

- the delete pass in `deploy-s3.ts` removes every `_astro/*` object the new
  build does not contain, the moment it is deployed;
- a page's HTML outlives its deploy in every cache — the CDN here ignores origin
  `max-age` (measured, see site-kn2), and even an honest cache or a browser
  keeps it for the five minutes `SHORT` allows.

`_astro/` names are content hashes: an old file never collides with a new one
and is only ever requested by old HTML. Keeping them costs a few kilobytes per
deploy that changes a stylesheet or script, and removes the failure entirely.

- [x] Other stale objects are still removed
- [x] The comment at the delete pass says why `_astro/` is kept
- [x] After a real deploy, a stylesheet from the previous build still answers 200

title: aliases is a field the schema accepts and nothing implements
description:
`aliases` is declared in the frontmatter schema, documented in design §4 as
"URL preservation on rename", and validated down to the shape of each path. It
is read by nothing.

```
src/schema/frontmatter.ts   declares and validates it
test/frontmatter.test.ts    tests that the validation works
(nothing else)              — src/redirects.ts, scripts/gen-redirects.ts and
                              the build never look at it
```

Set an alias on an article and it is checked for being a site-absolute path
with a trailing slash, and then silently ignored. No redirect is produced. The
old address 404s.

This is worse than a missing feature, because the field looks implemented: it is
in the schema an agent reads as its contract, it is in the design document, and
it fails loudly on a malformed value — every signal a writer gets says it works.

## Why it matters beyond the feature itself

It is what makes the migration map look permanent. `migration/redirects.yaml` is
a closed set of 49 addresses from a one-time import; it should never grow,
because a future rename is supposed to carry its old address in the article's
own frontmatter. With `aliases` dead, a rename has nowhere to go but that file,
and the migration artefact quietly becomes a routing table that keeps growing.

Fixing this is what lets `migration/` be frozen and eventually archived.

## Shape

The redirect renderer already turns a map into routing rules. Aliases are a
second source for the same map: collect `aliases` across the posts, expand each
into `from -> /posts/<slug>/`, and feed them through the same validation the
migration map goes through — R1's rules apply identically, and especially "a
redirect target must never itself be a redirect", which is now checkable across
both sources at once.

Two collisions must fail the build rather than resolve silently: an alias that
duplicates an entry in the migration map, and the same alias claimed by two
articles.

Related: `oh-my-portal-routing-rules-renderer-io1` — the renderer emits nginx
and the deploy is object storage. Both touch the same output stage, and doing
them together is probably cheaper than doing them apart.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Add `aliases: [/some-old-address/]` to any post's frontmatter.
2. Build.
3. Request `/some-old-address/`. Expected: a 301 to the post. Observed: nothing
   was generated for it at all.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] An `aliases` entry produces a real 301 to the article that declares it
- [x] Aliases and the migration map go through the same `validate()`; an alias colliding with the map, or claimed by two articles, fails generation
- [x] Chains across both sources are flattened to one hop; a cycle fails generation
- [x] Renaming an article that already has an old address needs no edit to `migration/`, covered by a test
- [x] `collectAliases()` is tested against real frontmatter
- [x] `gen-redirects.ts --coverage <old-addresses.txt>` fails when an old address is in neither `redirects` nor `unchanged`

description:

title: No story for images in content
description:
There is no image pipeline: nothing imports `astro:assets`, the frontmatter
schema has no `image()` field, and base.css styles a bare `img` and nothing else.
The maintainer wants to put pictures in posts.

§12's "no stock illustrations" is about decoration and does not forbid a diagram
or a screenshot inside an article — but the design doc says nothing about where
such a file lives, which is the actual question given the two-repository split
(§2): the engine has no content, so images arrive from the content repository
beside the markdown that references them.

The part that needs thought is the twin. An agent fetching `/posts/<slug>.md`
gets the raw markdown, so `![](./screenshot.png)` resolves against nothing on its
side. Either the projection rewrites image paths to absolute URLs, or the
convention is that authors write absolute paths and CI checks it — the first is
kinder, the second is simpler, and picking neither means the twins ship broken
links to precisely the readers §6 exists for.

Also to settle: whether images go through Astro's optimizer (a build-time cost
and a dependency on the file being importable) or are copied verbatim, and
whether alt text is required by the schema rather than by discipline.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] §4 says where an image file lives relative to the post that uses it
- [ ] An image referenced from a post renders in the HTML and resolves to a working absolute URL in the .md and .json twins
- [ ] A test covers the twin case, because a broken link there is invisible in a browser
- [ ] The alt-text rule is stated and enforced where it can be
- [ ] examples/posts carries one post with an image

title: Syntax highlighting has never been rendered once
description:
Neither example article contains a single fenced code block, so no build has ever
produced a highlighted block and nobody has looked at one. For a corpus about
homelab, kubernetes and security, a code block is the most-used element on the
site — and it is the one element the design has never seen.

What is actually there: astro.config.mjs sets no `markdown.shikiConfig`, so
Astro's default applies — Shiki with the `github-dark` theme, emitted as inline
styles on the element. On a near-white page that is a dark slab whose colours
come from nowhere in tokens.css and cannot be themed from it.

Design §12 says nothing about code at all, which is the root of it.

Decide and record: which theme (a light one, or a pair driven by the same tokens
as everything else), whether line numbers, whether a filename or language label
sits on the block, and how a long line behaves — the `pre { overflow-x: auto }`
in base.css handles it today, which is right, but it has never been tested with
real content.

The markdown twin is unaffected either way: it carries the raw fence, which is
what an agent wants.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] examples/posts carries a real article with fenced blocks in at least two languages, one with a long line
- [ ] A theme is chosen deliberately and configured in astro.config.mjs, not left at the default
- [ ] Code colours are legible on this page's ground and do not fight the tag palette
- [ ] The block has been looked at via npm run screenshot, on desktop and on a phone
- [ ] docs/design/portal.md §12 says what a code block looks like and why
